title: Write test cases for a login page BEYOND the happy path — valid/invalid username, invalid password, both invalid, empty fields, password masking, account lockout after N failed attempts, remember-me, session timeout, logout, SQL-injection and XSS inputs, password reset, browser compatibility, accessibility, and precise error messages — and what is the interviewer actually evaluating (that you think past "login works")?
shortTitle: Writing login page test cases beyond the happy path
topicTitle: Write test cases for a login page BEYOND the happy path

s1_definition.profdef: Writing login test cases beyond the happy path means systematically covering the full behavior surface of authentication rather than only the one valid-credentials success flow. It includes positive cases, many negative cases such as invalid username, invalid password, both invalid, and empty fields, security behaviors such as account lockout after a threshold of failed attempts and rejection of SQL-injection and cross-site-scripting inputs, session behaviors such as remember-me, session timeout, and logout, recovery flows such as password reset, non-functional checks such as browser compatibility and accessibility, and verification of precise, non-leaky error messages. The interviewer is evaluating whether you think like a tester who anticipates how a feature fails and is abused, not merely whether login works.
s1_definition.analogy: For the National Bank of India login screen, the happy path is Rajesh typing his correct username and password and getting in. But a real tester asks all the uncomfortable questions: what if the password is wrong, what if both fields are empty, what if someone tries the wrong password ten times to break in, does the password show as dots so a shoulder-surfer cannot read it, does "remember me" actually keep him logged in, does the session expire after inactivity so an unattended machine is safe, can an attacker type a database trick or a script into the username box, and does the error message say just "invalid credentials" rather than revealing whether the username exists. Covering all of these is what separates a real tester from someone who only checks that the front door opens for the right key.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Writing login test cases beyond the happy path means systematically covering the full behavior surface of authentication rather than only the one valid-credentials success flow. It includes positive cases, many negative cases such as invalid username, invalid password, both invalid, and empty fields, security behaviors such as account lockout after a threshold of failed attempts and rejection of SQL-injection and cross-site-scripting inputs, session behaviors such as remember-me, session timeout, and logout, recovery flows such as password reset, non-functional checks such as browser compatibility and accessibility, and verification of precise, non-leaky error messages. The interviewer is evaluating whether you think like a tester who anticipates how a feature fails and is abused, not merely whether login works.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** For the National Bank of India login screen, the happy path is Rajesh typing his correct username and password and getting in. But a real tester asks all the uncomfortable questions: what if the password is wrong, what if both fields are empty, what if someone tries the wrong password ten times to break in, does the password show as dots so a shoulder-surfer cannot read it, does "remember me" actually keep him logged in, does the session expire after inactivity so an unattended machine is safe, can an attacker type a database trick or a script into the username box, and does the error message say just "invalid credentials" rather than revealing whether the username exists. Covering all of these is what separates a real tester from someone who only checks that the front door opens for the right key.

**One line to remember:** Login testing beyond the happy path covers negatives, empty fields, masking, lockout, remember-me, session timeout, logout, injection and scripting attacks, password reset, browser and accessibility checks, and precise non-leaky error messages, because the interviewer is checking that you anticipate failure and abuse, not just success.

sections.s2_technical:
The happy path is a single case: valid username and valid password lead to a successful login and a redirect to the dashboard. Everything interesting is around it. The negative credential matrix covers valid username with invalid password, invalid username with any password, both invalid, and the correct rule that all failures return the same generic message so an attacker cannot tell which part was wrong, which is an account-enumeration defense. Empty-field cases cover empty username, empty password, both empty, and whitespace-only input, each expecting a clear validation message and no server call wasted.

Security behaviors are central for a bank. Account lockout after a threshold, for example five failed attempts, must lock the account for a cooldown or until reset, and you test the boundary precisely: the Nth attempt still allows, the N-plus-first triggers lockout, and a correct password during lockout is still refused. Input-injection cases feed SQL-injection payloads such as a quote-or-one-equals-one string and cross-site-scripting payloads such as a script tag into both fields, expecting the input to be safely rejected or escaped with no database error leaked and no script executed, confirming parameterized queries and output encoding. Password masking checks that the password renders as dots, that an optional show-password toggle works, and that the value is not exposed in the DOM in plain text or logged.

Session behaviors include remember-me, which should persist a secure, http-only, same-site cookie so the user stays logged in across browser restarts, and critically that it does not persist on a shared machine beyond its intended scope; session timeout, which should invalidate the session after a configured idle period and force re-authentication; and logout, which must invalidate the server session and clear cookies so the back button cannot reach an authenticated page. Recovery includes the password-reset flow, confirming a reset link is single-use and time-limited and that requesting a reset for a non-existent email does not reveal whether the account exists. Non-functional checks include browser compatibility across the supported matrix, for example Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, and accessibility, confirming the form is keyboard-navigable, has proper labels and ARIA roles, announces errors to screen readers, and meets contrast requirements. Finally, precise error messages must be user-friendly and non-leaky, never exposing stack traces, SQL errors, or whether a username exists.

The senior nuance, and what the interviewer is really assessing, is breadth of thinking and risk awareness. Anyone can test that login works. A strong tester enumerates failure modes, abuse cases, and quality attributes, prioritizes them by risk, which for a bank puts lockout, injection, session, and enumeration at the top, and writes each case with precise preconditions, steps, data, and an exact expected result including the exact message text and the security property being protected. Demonstrating that structure, grouping cases into positive, negative, security, session, recovery, and non-functional, is how you show you think past "login works."
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the login screen is the front door to everyone's money, so it must reject wrong credentials with a message that does not reveal whether the username exists. This is exactly the negative and enumeration-defense cases.

Problem 2 — Attackers will try passwords repeatedly and will paste database tricks and scripts into the fields. The system must lock the account after a threshold and safely neutralize injection and scripting input. This is exactly the lockout and injection cases.

Problem 3 — A logged-in session on an unattended machine is dangerous, so sessions must time out and logout must fully invalidate. This is exactly the session cases.

In the mini-project we model a login service that enforces these rules and a test catalog that exercises them, so the demo doubles as executable test cases. We define an `AuthResult`, a `LoginService` with generic error messages, lockout after five attempts, input sanitization, masking metadata, and session timeout, and a `LoginTestSuite` that runs positive, negative, security, and session cases and reports results.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a login service pre-loaded with Rajesh and Priya, and a suite of ten executable cases plus a note of the manual and end-to-end cases.

Step 1: The positive case logs in Rajesh with correct credentials and expects SUCCESS, confirming the happy path still works.

Step 2: The negative cases submit a wrong password for a valid user and any password for an unknown user, and both return the same generic invalid-credentials result, proving the system does not reveal whether the username exists.

Step 3: The empty-field case submits blank fields and expects a validation error before any credential check.

Step 4: The security lockout case fails four times, which are still allowed as invalid, then the fifth failure flips the account to LOCKED, and a subsequent correct password is still refused while locked, verifying the boundary exactly.

Step 5: The injection and scripting cases paste a SQL payload and a script tag, both of which the service blocks without leaking any database error, and the masking and session-timeout properties are asserted. The demo then lists the remaining manual and end-to-end cases such as remember-me, logout invalidation, single-use reset links, the browser matrix, and accessibility.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Login form input {username, password}
    │
    ▼
  Empty? ──yes──→ VALIDATION_ERROR (no server credential call)
    │ no
    ▼
  Malicious payload? ──yes──→ BLOCKED_INPUT (no SQL leak, no script run)
    │ no
    ▼
  Account locked? ──yes──→ LOCKED ("reset your password")
    │ no
    ▼
  Credentials match?
    ├─ no  → failures++  → failures>=5? ──yes──→ LOCKED
    │                                    └─no──→ INVALID_CREDENTIALS (generic)
    └─ yes → SUCCESS → create session (secure/httpOnly cookie, 10-min timeout)
                         │
                         ├─ remember-me → persistent secure cookie
                         ├─ idle 10 min → session invalidated
                         └─ logout → session destroyed, cookie cleared
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I write login test cases I start from the position that the happy path, valid username and valid password leading to the dashboard, is a single case, and that everything valuable lies around it. I group the rest into families. The negative credential matrix covers valid user with wrong password, unknown user, both invalid, and the crucial rule that every failure returns the same generic message so an attacker cannot enumerate which usernames exist. Empty-field cases cover blank and whitespace-only input with clear validation before any server call. Security cases cover account lockout after a threshold such as five attempts, tested exactly at the boundary so the fifth failure locks and a correct password is still refused while locked, and injection cases that paste SQL and cross-site-scripting payloads into both fields and expect them safely neutralized with no database error or script execution. Session cases cover remember-me using a secure, http-only, same-site cookie, session timeout after idle, and logout that fully invalidates the server session so the back button cannot reach a protected page. Recovery covers a single-use, time-limited password-reset link that does not reveal whether an email exists. Non-functional cases cover the supported browser matrix and accessibility, keyboard navigation, labels and ARIA roles, screen-reader error announcements, and contrast. And throughout I assert precise, non-leaky error messages that never expose stack traces or SQL.

What I believe the interviewer is really evaluating is whether I think past "login works." Anyone can confirm the front door opens for the right key; a strong tester enumerates how the feature fails and how it is abused, prioritizes by risk, which for a bank puts lockout, injection, session handling, and enumeration defense at the top, and writes each case with precise preconditions, data, steps, and an exact expected result including the message text and the security property being protected.

At the National Bank of India I owned the login test suite, and I caught two real issues this way: a response that revealed whether a username existed, which I flagged as an account-enumeration vulnerability, and a logout that did not invalidate the server session so the back button still showed account data. Both were missed by happy-path testing and both mattered because this was the front door to customers' money. Being able to lay out these case families and explain the risk behind each, especially the security and session ones, is exactly how I show an interviewer I test like someone who protects a bank, not someone who checks a checkbox.
